payload.input:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Belief, to believe

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'belief' or 'to believe' (Greek pisteuo, Hebrew aman) is understood not as mere intellectual acknowledgment but as saving faith: personal trust in, reliance upon, and commitment to God and specifically to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. It is treated as the divinely appointed means of receiving salvation, justification, and eternal life, involving assent to the truth of the gospel, trust of the heart, and entrustment of oneself to Christ. Classical Protestant theology often analyzes it into three elements: notitia (knowledge of the content), assensus (assent that it is true), and fiducia (personal trust). Belief is thus the relational counterpart of God's grace: grace offers, faith receives.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 3:16 - 'whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life'",
    "John 1:12 - to all who believed in his name he gave the right to become children of God",
    "John 20:30-31 - these are written that you may believe and by believing have life",
    "Acts 16:31 - 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved'",
    "Romans 10:9-10 - believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead and you will be saved",
    "Romans 4:3-5 and Genesis 15:6 - Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness",
    "Ephesians 2:8-9 - by grace you have been saved through faith",
    "Hebrews 11:1, 6 - faith defined; without faith it is impossible to please God",
    "Mark 1:15 - 'repent and believe the good news'",
    "John 6:29 - the work of God is to believe in the one he has sent",
    "Habakkuk 2:4 - the righteous shall live by his faith (cited in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as intellectual assent only (accepting propositions as true). Christian interpreters almost universally cite this as an inadequate or counterfeit form of belief rather than the biblical ideal, pointing out that 'even the demons believe—and shudder.' It functions as a recognized foil to true saving faith.",
      "basis": [
        "James 2:19 - demons believe and tremble",
        "James 2:14-26 - faith without works is dead",
        "John 2:23-25 - many believed in his name, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them",
        "John 12:42-43 - rulers believed but would not confess him"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as faithfulness, fidelity, or allegiance (pistis rendered as loyalty to Christ as King rather than a moment of inner trust). This is a growing scholarly emphasis (e.g., work associated with the 'pistis as allegiance' discussion and pistis Christou debates) and resonates with the Hebrew aman/emunah background of steadfastness.",
      "basis": [
        "Habakkuk 2:4 - emunah as faithfulness/steadfastness",
        "Romans 1:5 and 16:26 - 'the obedience of faith'",
        "Galatians 2:16, 20 and Romans 3:22 - pistis Christou debate ('faith in Christ' vs. 'faithfulness of Christ')",
        "Revelation 2:10 - be faithful unto death"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as an ongoing life of obedient discipleship inseparable from works (Catholic, Orthodox, and Wesleyan emphases; faith formed by love, fides caritate formata), as opposed to a single decisive act of trust. This differs materially from strict 'faith alone' readings in how belief relates to works and perseverance.",
      "basis": [
        "James 2:24 - a person is justified by works and not by faith alone",
        "Galatians 5:6 - faith working through love",
        "John 3:36 - whoever believes has life; whoever does not obey shall not see life",
        "Matthew 7:21 - not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom",
        "Colossians 1:23 - continue in the faith, stable and steadfast"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as a sovereign gift produced entirely by God (Reformed/monergist reading), versus belief as a free human response enabled by grace (Arminian/synergist reading). Both agree on the meaning of belief as trust but differ on its origin; this is an intra-Christian dispute about mechanism rather than symbolism.",
      "basis": [
        "Ephesians 2:8 - 'and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God'",
        "Philippians 1:29 - it has been granted to you to believe",
        "John 6:44 - no one can come unless the Father draws him",
        "Acts 13:48 - as many as were appointed to eternal life believed",
        "Deuteronomy 30:19 and Joshua 24:15 - choose whom you will serve (invoked for free response)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as mystical or existential encounter—an experiential union with or leap toward God that transcends propositional content (associated with mystical traditions and existentialist theology such as Kierkegaard and Tillich's 'ultimate concern').",
      "basis": [
        "Mark 9:24 - 'I believe; help my unbelief'",
        "Hebrews 11:1 - assurance of things hoped for, conviction of things not seen",
        "2 Corinthians 5:7 - we walk by faith, not by sight"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "'Belief/believe' is less a symbol than a core theological concept, and its central meaning—personal trust in God/Christ that receives salvation—is among the most settled definitions in Christian interpretation across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions. The recognizable disputes concern its components and implications (assent vs. trust vs. allegiance; relation to works; divine gift vs. human response), not its basic sense. A widely repeated teaching point is the distinction between 'believing that' (assent, which demons share, James 2:19) and 'believing in/into' (Greek pisteuo eis, entrusting oneself), especially prominent in the Gospel of John, which uses the verb 'believe' nearly 100 times while never using the noun 'faith.'"
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "Belief is most commonly understood not as a symbolic image but as faith: accepting the truth of God’s revelation and personally trusting, relying upon, and committing oneself to God—especially to Jesus Christ—for salvation.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 3:16–18 — believing in the Son is contrasted with unbelief and associated with eternal life.",
    "John 6:28–29, 35, 40 — believing in Christ is portrayed as coming to him and receiving life.",
    "John 20:30–31 — the Gospel’s signs are recorded so that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ and have life in his name.",
    "Acts 16:30–31 — belief in the Lord Jesus is presented as the response leading to salvation.",
    "Romans 4:3–5, 18–24 — Abraham’s belief exemplifies trusting God’s promise and is reckoned as righteousness.",
    "Romans 10:9–13 — heart-belief and confession of Jesus as Lord are associated with salvation.",
    "Galatians 2:16 — justification is associated with faith in Jesus Christ rather than works of the law.",
    "Hebrews 11:1, 6 — faith entails confidence in what is hoped for and trust in God’s existence and faithfulness.",
    "James 2:14–26 — living faith is distinguished from bare intellectual assent by its resulting actions."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as intellectual assent: accepting a proposition as true, without necessarily implying personal trust, obedience, or saving commitment.",
      "basis": [
        "James 2:19 explicitly describes demons as believing that God is one, showing that belief can denote factual assent without saving faith.",
        "John 12:42–43 describes people who believed in Jesus yet would not openly confess him.",
        "Acts 8:13, 18–24 has often been used in discussions of belief that may be superficial or deficient."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as allegiance or loyal commitment to Jesus as Lord, emphasizing fidelity and embodied obedience more than inward assent.",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 10:9 connects belief with confessing Jesus as Lord.",
        "John 3:36 can be translated or understood in terms of believing in versus disobeying the Son.",
        "Romans 1:5 and 16:26 speak of the “obedience of faith.”",
        "Philippians 2:9–11 presents confession of Jesus’ lordship in royal and covenantal terms."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as divinely enabled faith or a gift of grace rather than primarily an autonomous human decision.",
      "basis": [
        "John 6:44, 65 stresses the Father’s enabling of those who come to Christ.",
        "Acts 13:48 associates belief with appointment to eternal life.",
        "Ephesians 2:8–9 is frequently cited in debates over whether faith itself is included in God’s gift.",
        "Philippians 1:29 speaks of belief in Christ as something granted."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Belief as confident expectation that prayer, confession, or inner certainty will produce a desired outcome, especially healing or material blessing.",
      "basis": [
        "Mark 11:22–24 is frequently interpreted as requiring unwavering belief in prayer.",
        "Matthew 17:20 links faith with apparently impossible outcomes.",
        "James 5:15 speaks of the prayer of faith in connection with healing."
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad Christian consensus that “belief” centrally involves faith or trust, particularly trust in God and Christ. There is no single settled symbolic interpretation because the biblical words translated “believe” normally function as direct theological and relational language rather than as a conventional symbol. Disagreement concerns whether particular occurrences emphasize factual assent, personal trust, loyalty, obedience, divine enablement, or some combination of these."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "Personal trust/reliance upon God (especially Jesus Christ) for salvation, eternal life, and relationship with God, going beyond mere intellectual assent to include commitment and dependence",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 3:16-18",
    "John 20:31",
    "Acts 16:31",
    "Romans 3:22-28",
    "Romans 10:9-10",
    "Ephesians 2:8-9",
    "Hebrews 11:1,6",
    "Mark 1:15",
    "Galatians 2:16"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Intellectual assent or cognitive agreement with doctrines/facts about God or Christ (without necessarily implying trust or transformation)",
      "basis": [
        "James 2:19",
        "John 2:23-25",
        "Acts 8:13"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Covenant faithfulness, loyalty, or obedience (pistis as fidelity rather than primarily mental belief)",
      "basis": [
        "Habakkuk 2:4 (as cited in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11)",
        "Romans 1:5",
        "Galatians 5:6",
        "Hebrews 3:12-19"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Blind or unexamined acceptance without evidence or reason",
      "basis": [
        "Popular caricatures or critiques rather than primary biblical texts"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, 'belief/to believe' (Greek pisteuō/pistis) is overwhelmingly treated as saving faith centered on Christ; scholarly nuances around 'faithfulness' exist but do not displace the dominant pastoral and confessional emphasis on trust for salvation. The term is largely functional/theological rather than a free-floating symbol like water or light."
}

BOOK ENTRY
Receiving God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it. Bare assent can recognize a fact — demons believe and tremble — but saving belief obeys the word believed, and persistent refusal to obey exposes unbelief.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: personal trust in Christ, not mere assent — the instrument that receives salvation.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Mark 1:27; John 3:36; 12:42-43; Rom 10:16; Heb 3:18-19; Jas 2:19-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Mark 1:27 — And they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him.
John 3:36 — He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.
John 12:42 — Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue:
John 12:43 — For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Romans 10:16 — But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report?
Hebrews 3:18 — And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest, but to them that believed not?
Hebrews 3:19 — So we see that they could not enter in because of unbelief.
James 2:19 — Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.
James 2:20 — But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?
James 2:21 — Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?
James 2:22 — Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

- MATCH: substantially the same meaning as the recognizable consensus.
- REFINED: compatible with the consensus but materially sharper, narrower,
  broader, or more precisely supported.
- DIVERGENT: contradicts or displaces a recognizable common interpretation.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus covers the book's central claim; the book
  stakes a meaning not represented by the blind responses.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
